question.prompt: Why can Sam not answer the engineer's first question?

options.text: he has never visited the creek
He has only observed sunny afternoons

question.explanation: The engineer asks about conditions after rain, outside Sam's observation period. The gap concerns the range of evidence rather than Sam's ability to map it.

stimulus.title: The bridge notebook
stimulus.body:
When the old footbridge closed, Sam began recording how people crossed the creek. A cyclist pushed her bicycle through the shallow ford. A man with a walking frame turned back. Three children took the long road past the shops. Sam drew each route in a notebook.

At the planning meeting, he expected the adults to admire his neat map. Instead, the engineer asked which routes people could use after rain. Sam had no answer. His observations all came from sunny afternoons.

The next wet morning he returned with his father. The ford had vanished beneath brown water. On his map, Sam drew a dotted line around it and added the date. He did not erase the earlier routes. At the second meeting, his map was untidier, with notes squeezed into the margins. This time he could explain why the shortest route on paper was not always an available route in practice.

workedSolution: The engineer asks about conditions after rain, outside Sam's observation period.
The gap concerns the range of evidence rather than Sam's ability to map it.

question.prompt: How many packets may a visitor take at one visit to the seed library?
question.explanation: The notice explicitly sets a limit of three packets per visit. Donating is encouraged but is not a condition of borrowing.

stimulus.title: The seed library notice
stimulus.body:
Borrow a packet, grow a possibility.

Our neighbourhood seed library opens on Saturday. Anyone may take up to three packets at a visit. You do not need to return seeds to borrow, but successful growers are invited to donate fresh, dry seeds from clearly identified plants. Please label donations with the plant name and harvest month. We cannot accept unidentified seeds or seeds from invasive plants.

Packets are sorted by planting season, not alphabetically. A blue dot means the plant needs a container at least thirty centimetres deep; it does not mean the plant needs extra water. Ask a volunteer if the planting directions are unclear.

The first collection is small, so a packet is an invitation to experiment, not a promise of a full harvest. Keep a record of what grows and share it on the noticeboard. Even an unsuccessful attempt can tell the next gardener something useful about local conditions.

Donating is encouraged but is not a condition of borrowing.

question.prompt: What was wrong with the station clock before the repair?
question.explanation: The opening sentence gives its consistent five-minute lead. The later surprise follows correction of that error, not a slow or stopped clock.

stimulus.title: A clock that gained a story
stimulus.body:
For years the station clock had been five minutes fast. Commuters joked that it was trying to make them punctual. Then a technician reset it. The next morning, people gathered under its newly accurate hands and compared watches.

'It used to be reliable,' one traveller complained.

'It is reliable now,' the technician said.

Both were using the word differently. The traveller had known exactly how far wrong the clock was and had adjusted mentally. The repair removed that familiar error. For a few days, old habits made accurate time feel surprising.

The station manager put up a notice: 'Clock corrected on Monday. Please check your usual adjustment.' By Friday, the jokes had changed. People said the clock had finally decided to catch the train itself. The technician kept the old maintenance note, not as an instruction for the next repair, but as a reminder that changing a machine can also require changing the habits around it.

workedSolution: The opening sentence gives its consistent five-minute lead.
The later surprise follows correction of that error, not a slow or stopped clock.
